The platform is built so that no single defect — a buggy query filter, corrupted stored data, a misbehaving client, a replayed token — can widen access on its own. Every request path crosses at least two independent enforcement layers that would each have to fail for an unauthorized action to succeed. Internal faults are logged, not leaked.
When an internal invariant is violated, the full detail (CRIs, ids) goes to the server log for operators, and the caller receives a generic error indistinguishable from a routine failure.
Kinotic runs three servers, one per plane — system, organization and application — and each has its own public hosts, gateway,
and session cookie. What a server serves is fixed in its server module, so isolation comes from what code runs behind which host, not from configuration flags.

The derivation defends its own inputs:
Ids are validated before they form a zone.
An organization or application id must be a single dot-free label. A crafted id containing a dot would shift the
label structure — letting one (org, app) pair produce the same zone as a different pair plus a sub-zone — so such an id fails authentication instead of widening access.

An address without a zone carries no isolation boundary, so only participants allowed to send anywhere may address it.
Each server serves its own zones.

A server's zone partitioning narrows every participant's rules to the zones that server reaches and hosts: the management server never routes to an application's zone or lets a runtime publish into one, and the app server never reaches

Every frame on a connection is checked against the participant's zones — authenticating once does not exempt any later send or subscribe:

No external connection may subscribe in those zones, so no external node can register itself as a platform service and intercept calls.
A browser authenticates with one session cookie per API host, and every login in the session is bound to the page that made it:
A login authenticates only its own page.
, or for a same-origin request, which carries none, the origin of its

. A page that shares the cookie's site without having logged in, such as a published UI on a sibling host, finds no login under its origin, so it cannot ride another page's session. Logging out ends only the calling page's login; the session ends once no page's login, and no sign-in another page has in progress, remains.
A session is bound to the host that issued it.

Each login records the host it was established on, and a session presented on any other host is destroyed and the request refused, so a cookie replayed by hand against another API host authenticates nothing.
A redirect login binds to the page that started it.
An identity provider returns the browser with a top-level navigation that carries no

, so the flow records the starting page's origin when it begins; the completed login is bound to that page and the browser is sent back there. On the management server the flow records the page only when it is the portal or
names it, and a flow started anywhere else returns to the portal, so a page outside the pattern learns nothing from where a flow lands, not even whether an email already has an account.
An application's users sign in only from its own UIs.
The app server starts a login, by password or through an identity provider, only from a page whose host is one of the application's sites,

under the sites domain, with or without a tenant before the application, and its CORS pattern holds pages to the sites domain. A UI of another application shares that domain, so without the check it could start a single sign-on the identity provider completes without a prompt and hold the login on this application's host.
The tool lookup queries Elasticsearch with the caller's zone visibility filter, narrowed to the zones this server reaches — a tool outside them is not found at all, exactly as if it did not exist.
Before the call is sent, the invoker re-checks the resolved CRI against the same
the STOMP path enforces. If the stored directory data or the visibility query were ever wrong, the dispatch is refused, the CRIs are logged as a server fault, and the caller sees an unknown tool.
The surrounding surface is hardened the same way:
Tool names are always minted, never parsed.

A name is derived from the service's qualified name and function, making it unique system wide; no override exists, and nothing ever parses a name apart to make a decision — resolution is a caller-scoped directory query and authorization reads the zone from the stored CRI, so the name is never a trust input.
The tool listing query excludes the CRI at the Elasticsearch
level, so the internal address never leaves the data store for a listing.
Duplicate names are refused, not resolved.

Minted names are unique system wide, so more than one match for a name means the directory index is corrupted. The platform never picks a winner: the providing CRIs are logged for operators and the caller receives a generic internal error.

Linking a GitHub account stores the record that authorizes every later repository operation for that org — repo creation, pushes, token minting all trace back to it — so the bind itself crosses three independent proofs before it is persisted:
The state token binds the round-trip to the org.
mints a single-use, 10-minute state bound to the caller's organization;
consumes it atomically and rejects a state staged for a different org. A replayed or forged callback dies here.
The user-authorization code binds the round-trip to a GitHub user.

The App requests user authorization (OAuth) during installation, so GitHub's post-install redirect carries a code that only the person who authenticated at GitHub in that browser can produce. The server exchanges it — using the GitHub App's own OAuth credential — for that user's access token.
GitHub attests the user controls the installation.
in the redirect is browser-supplied and therefore attacker-controlled; installation ids are small sequential integers, and the App itself can resolve
of its installations, so no App-credential lookup can vet one. Instead the server asks GitHub which installations of this App the authorizing user can access (

with the user's token) and persists the binding only when the claimed id — with a matching App id — appears on that list. Claiming another customer's installation fails with an authorization error and nothing is stored.
The account login and type stored on the binding are read from the attested
entry, never from a lookup made with the App's own credentials.

JWT scope claims are cross-checked against the user record.

claim resolves to — a token minted before the user was moved or re-scoped is rejected even though its signature verifies.
Credential failures are also uniform: an unknown email and a wrong password produce the same
error, so the login surface cannot be used to enumerate which accounts exist.
